title: Russia bombards Kyiv and other cities in onslaught testing Ukraine's defenses
description: Russia bombarded cities across Ukraine with missiles and drones in an overnight onslaught that ran into the daylight hours of Thursday, when explosions echoed around Kyiv through the morning.  Ukraine...
fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia bombarded cities across Ukraine with missiles and drones in an overnight onslaught that ran into the daylight hours of Thursday, when explosions echoed around Kyiv through the morning.

Ukraine is desperately short of U.S.-made Patriot air defense missiles that can counter Russia's ballistic missiles, and Moscow's fast-flying jet-powered drones have brought another challenge since the Russian military's full-scale invasion began 4½ years ago.

Ukrainian officials say Russia builds up missile stocks and launches major attacks every few days, hoping to exhaust Ukrainian defenses through the sheer weight of numbers. In response, Ukraine has hit high-profile targets on Russian soil as the countries inflict mutual destruction.

The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces carried out a "massive" strike on targets in nine Ukrainian cities that began after nightfall on Wednesday. It described the targets as military-related, including industrial facilities, oil refineries, logistics hubs and port infrastructure.

Civilian areas, including apartment buildings, suffered damage. The barrage killed a 78-year-old woman in the southern Zaporizhzhia region and another person in the northern Kharkiv region, with at least 14 people reported wounded elsewhere, Ukrainian officials said.

"Russia continues to invest in missiles and in expanding its war, and that means more countermeasures are needed," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media, noting promises earlier this week by European countries to provide more air defense assistance.

"It is important that these (measures) are also supplemented by additional ballistic missile defense packages" through European purchases of weapons from the United States, he said.

Though the Russian Defense Ministry insisted only war-related targets were attacked, Russia appears determined to hurt Ukrainian businesses and dent the country's economy through attacks on private enterprise after Ukraine's long-range drone strikes caused financial difficulties for Moscow.

Russian drones hit three major distribution centers, destroying depots belonging to a toy store chain and a confectionery company, and damaging another run by an electronics retailer, the companies said.

In addition, Moscow continued its efforts to wreck the Ukrainian power grid before the freezing winter months.

Four powerful glide bombs destroyed generating equipment at the southern Kherson region's combined heat and power plant, forcing it to shut down, its operator Naftogaz said.

Zelenskyy was due to visit neighboring Moldova on Thursday to mark its national day commemorating its 1991 declaration of independence from the Soviet Union. Ukraine announced its independence the same year.

Russia's neighbors in Eastern Europe are concerned its invasion of Ukraine could trigger a wider conflict, and drones flying into its airspace have fueled jitters.

Moldova's Ministry of Defense said Thursday that five drones breached its airspace overnight, but it didn't specify who fired them.

Ukraine's air force said defenses shot down or suppressed seven Russian ballistic missiles, though it didn't say how they achieved that.

Four districts of Kyiv were hit during the night, damaging residential buildings, a school and a medical facility, though no casualties were reported, city police said.

Russian forces struck industrial facilities as well as energy infrastructure in Ukraine's central Poltava region, said Vitalii Diakivnych, head of the Poltava regional military administration.

The southern Odesa region also came under a major Russian attack lasting more than seven hours, according to Oleh Kiper, head of the Odesa regional military administration.

The barrage damaged a 16-story residential building and two educational facilities as well as a grain elevator, he said. Odesa is a key port for Ukraine's vital exports of grain and other agricultural products.

Some trains were delayed by more than 17 hours following the attack, according to Ukrainian state rail company Ukrzaliznysia.

Ukraine has also fired hundreds of long-range drones almost nightly at targets in Russia.

Ukraine's General Staff said that plane-launched missiles hit Russia's main and backup command posts near the eastern city of Donetsk, where Ukrainian defenders are under pressure from a Russian push.

The Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday that its air defenses shot down 267 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions, the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula, the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

After razing huge warehouses in recent months belonging to Wildberries, Russia's biggest online retailer, Ukrainian drones are now taking aim at Ozon, the country's second-largest e-commerce company.

Ozon initially said that its logistics facilities in the cities of Orenburg and Ufa were attacked, but neither of the premises caught fire. A later alteration to the company statement said that only the Ufa site was attacked, while the Orenburg facility was evacuated because of an alert, but resumed normal operations.

title: US officials tie cyclospora outbreak involving iceberg lettuce to 3 more states
description: Parasitic illness cases linked to recalled iceberg lettuce have now been confirmed in 20 states, federal health officials said Thursday, expanding the scope of the largest outbreak of its kind in the ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Parasitic illness cases linked to recalled iceberg lettuce have now been confirmed in 20 states, federal health officials said Thursday, expanding the scope of the largest outbreak of its kind in the U.S.

The Food and Drug Administration said government scientists have now identified cases in three additional states: Georgia, Tennessee and Texas.

The tally of people sickened by the parasite is now 11,458, up from about 10,900 reported last week.

The FDA, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health officials have focused their investigation on lettuce grown at a farm in central Mexico operated by Taylor Farms, a major U.S. produce supplier.

The FDA said its staffers are continuing to inspect and test produce at the farm, in cooperation with officials from the Mexican government. The U.S. agency said it "remains confident that all recalled iceberg lettuce related to this specific cyclospora outbreak is off the market."

Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that commonly causes watery diarrhea "with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements," according to the CDC. Outbreaks tend to occur most often in the late spring and summer.

The heat-loving parasite infects the bowels and spreads through feces. The illness, called cyclosporiasis, is less common than foodborne illnesses caused by other germs, including salmonella and E. coli. Many cyclospora cases are never linked to a specific food or other source.

Earlier this week, the CDC reported that there have been about 29,000 confirmed or suspected cyclospora cases in the U.S. this year. There have been 922 hospitalizations, according to the agency. Previously, the worst year in the U.S. for infections was 2019, when about 4,700 illnesses were reported nationally.

The boater charged in the crash that killed a 24-year-old former student athlete was intoxicated and dancing with his hands off the wheel when he steered a stolen boat into a Boston pier, prosecutors said.

Lawrence Shieh, 40, of Boston, was indicted by a Suffolk County grand jury on multiple charges in connection with the May 13 crash that killed Elizabeth "Lizzie" Dankert, 24, and injured two of her friends. He is charged with one count of involuntary manslaughter, one count of boat OUI causing death, two counts of boat OUI causing serious bodily injury, using a boat without authority, and a Logan International Airport security zone violation.

"That night, Lawrence Shieh drank a mix of alcoholic beverages at the ReelHouse with friends and several other bars in the Seaport," Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden told reporters. "Blood testing after the crash recorded his blood-alcohol at .20, or more than twice the .08 legal limit here in Massachusetts."

The boat, which was not equipped with exterior lighting, had been docked at Freedom Boat Club in Boston's Seaport District before it was taken without permission. Although Shieh held membership in the club, he had no authorization to remove the vessel. Hayden said cellphone footage — including video recorded on Dankert's phone — captured the moments leading up to the deadly crash.

The boat then crashed nearly head-on into Pier 4R at Logan.

"Recovered data from the boat navigation system indicates that the boat was traveling at a dangerously excessive speed for the area of 36 mph at the time of the crash," Hayden said.

Dankert struck her head and died as a result of blunt force injuries. The other two women and Shieh suffered non-life-threatening injuries.

title: Largest ever ‘map’ of autism may hold clues for new targeted therapies
description: Scientists are getting a step closer to understanding exactly how autism develops in the brain – and what might work to treat it.
fullText:
Scientists are getting a step closer to understanding exactly how autism develops in the brain – and what might work to treat it.

Using artificial intelligence and data on tiny brains grown in the lab, researchers have mapped out the ways in which certain genetic mutations that are associated with autism can rewire the brain and lead to the condition. The molecular map, published Thursday in the journal Science, could help inform more targeted therapies for autism.

"You need this insight to ultimately develop drugs, and we've generated a map now that is providing essentially the molecular underpinnings of autism and pointing us in a multitude of different directions for ultimate drug discovery," said study author Dr. Nevan Krogan, professor at the University of California, San Francisco and senior investigator at the nonprofit Gladstone Institutes

"The hope would be at some point you'd be looking back and saying, 'Ah, this map led to X, Y, and Z, and therefore we have now the first-ever treatment to autism.' That's the vision, and I believe that's going to come to fruition at some point in the future," Krogan said.

For decades, developing effective treatments for autism has been a scientific puzzle.

Since there are more than 250 genes associated with autism spectrum disorder, finding a treatment that targets the genetic roots of the disorder is equivalent to seeking a single key for hundreds of different locks.

But now, the new study reveals how many of these diverse genetic mutations physically connect and rewire protein interactions in the developing brain, driving the emergence of autism. Proteins are molecules that physically build and help maintain the brain. So instead of needing hundreds of different drugs to target the genes themselves, scientists now have a blueprint to target the protein interactions instead.

"When you have the genes and the mutations, that's just a list. That's a parts list," said Krogan, who also serves as director of the Quantitative Biosciences Institute at UCSF.

"What you need to do is have a wiring diagram of that parts list, and that's where you need to go to the proteins and understand how the proteins talk to one another, and understand when you put a mutation in a protein, what does it do to the protein-protein interactions?" he said. "So, understanding that will point you down therapeutic roads that you just could not have ever imagined if you were simply just looking at the genes and the mutation."

Krogan said that his colleagues and he already have three programs currently underway to develop potential new therapies, using insights from the new study.

To build the autism map, researchers from the University of California, San Francisco systematically mapped out how genetic mutations tied to autism may influence interactions between proteins in the brain. They found more than 1,800 protein-protein interactions tied to autism, among which 87% of those interactions had never been seen before.

The researchers created the map in the presence of the genetic mutations to understand how the proteins were "rewired" and then used an artificial intelligence system called AlphaFold to prioritize key mutations that were then studied in lab-grown brain organoids.

"AI is allowing us to study proteins that we could never have even dreamed of even a couple of years ago, and it's providing an unprecedented light being shone on autism, the underlying biology behind autism," Krogan said.

The map is "the largest that has ever been done on autism," he said. "It's the largest map of its kind for any neuropsychiatric disorder, but it's also the largest mutant map that's ever been generated for any disease area."

The new study "is really exciting in that it represents the most systematic protein-level view of autism risk we've had to date," Fikri Birey, assistant professor in the Department of Human Genetics at Emory University School of Medicine, who was not involved in the study, wrote in an email.

"In the future, it may be possible to identify drugs that stabilize disrupted protein complexes or block pathological interactions, rather than trying to correct every individual autism-causing mutation," Birey wrote, adding that the new study findings could help inform the disease-modeling research conducted in his own lab.

While the new study offers a map of molecular pathways through which autism may develop, it may not be definitive for every person with autism or every type of the disorder – as the study remains most directly relevant to people with profound autism, who account for about 30% of people with autism spectrum disorder.

"So those are ones that, for example, need 24-hour care," Krogan said.

However, he added that the study's findings on protein-protein interactions still could help inform other neuropsychiatric conditions too, including schizophrenia, obsessive-compulsive disorder and tic disorders, as well as other diseases including cancer.

Autism experts and advocates alike have applauded the new study, as it may open the door for more research into potential treatments.

"Today's study shows where different autism genes converge on shared biological pathways, and those shared pathways could ultimately give us therapeutic targets relevant to much larger groups of autistic people, including people without an identified genetic cause. That is nothing short of a huge watershed moment for autism science," Alison Singer, president of the nonprofit Autism Science Foundation, who was not involved in the new study, wrote in an email.

"For families of people with profound autism like mine, this is the kind of scientific advance we have been waiting for and praying for. Many people with profound autism have rare genetic variants and the promise of precision medicine has always been that understanding those variants would eventually allow us to move beyond treating symptoms and behaviors, and begin addressing the underlying biology," Singer wrote.

"There is still a lot of work ahead and these discoveries today need to be translated into drug candidates and then tested for safety and effectiveness, but the path from genetic discovery to treatment has just become much clearer."

While the new research is "exciting," the nonprofit Autism Speak's chief science officer Dr. Andy Shih cautioned that translating the study's findings into potential therapies would take a significant amount of time.

"Translating these kinds of discoveries into therapies is a long process," Shih wrote in an email. "This study provides valuable insights into potential targets, but much more research is needed before these findings can lead to clinical applications."

Autism has become a major focus of the second Trump administration's Department of Health and Human Services, under which the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee (IACC) helps develop and update the national strategic plan for autism research. A new draft plan is up for a committee vote on Thursday.

Singer said that she is not convinced that the new draft plan will usher in more research on the biological targets of autism like what was found in the new study. Rather, she said that she has some concerns that the Trump administration may steer attention away from the current science and instead focus on an unproven link between vaccines and autism.

The federal plan for autism research "deemphasizes genetics, neurodevelopment, and brain biology in favor of a broad injury model that is not consistent with the direction of contemporary autism science," Singer wrote. "Redirecting limited federal research investments away from the strongest biological evidence will slow scientific progress precisely when these types of unprecedented opportunities for therapeutic development are emerging."

But Shih of Autism Speaks said that he expects the new IACC strategic plan will include more research into the genetic changes linked with autism.

"There is significant interest in understanding developmental trajectories in the new IACC strategic plan," he wrote. "And I would expect that continued investment in large-scale, data-driven approaches will lead to more studies examining how genetic factors contribute to autism and affect development."

title: Welcome to the ‘upper-middle-class trap’: why $300,000 a year doesn’t feel like winning anymore
description: Investopedia put a $5 million price tag on the American Dream, but Nick Maggiulli says six-figure earners are more financially fragile than they look.
fullText:
Over the last year, Nick Maggiulli has come to what he calls an unsettling realization: The upper-middle class is caught in a trap, and many of them don't even realize it.

The chief operating officer of Ritholtz Wealth Management has spent the better part of a year building the case in pieces on his blog, Of Dollars and Data—first arguing private school isn't worth the cost despite its price tag, then that premium travel experiences have grown crowded while remaining expensive in "The Death of the Amex Lounge." He previously talked to Fortune about his book, The Wealth Ladder, and his growing belief "something weird's going on" with the upper-middle class in the U.S. economy.

In an April essay, he pulled the threads together and gave the phenomenon a name: the "upper-middle-class trap," in which people earning roughly $200,000 to $400,000 a year are working more and relaxing less to buy products and services of declining quality.

His evidence includes new single-family homes shrinking in average size by 12% between 2014 and 2024, even as the price per square foot surged 74%, according to LendingTree data. A home near a public elementary school with a top GreatSchools rating costs 78.6% more than a comparable home in the surrounding county. Homebuyers who win bidding wars end up worse off: One study found their purchases produced 6.9% lower annualized returns than homes bought without competition. In higher education, the number of college applicants has jumped 78% since 2015 even as acceptance rates at elite schools have collapsed, driving tuition and private-school costs up roughly twice as fast as overall inflation.

The mechanism Maggiulli describes is a "financial arms race": Every individual decision is rational, but collectively the competition for the same scarce positional goods lowers everyone's quality of life while draining their bank accounts.

One accelerant, he argues, is nearly impossible to opt out of. Citing Brookings Institution data from November 2025, he notes AI usage rises from 9% among earners below $30,000 to 34% among those earning $100,000 or more. High earners, worried AI threatens their careers, are forced to adopt it just to defend their position—a "Red Queen" dynamic in which everyone runs faster just to stay in place.

"If AI doubled everyone's productivity overnight," he writes, "suddenly someone with half your skill would be able to compete with you just by using AI."

His prescribed exit is blunt: Stop competing for positional goods that don't materially improve your life. Send your kids to good public schools, fly economy, buy a smaller, affordable house. His test for any big purchase: "Am I buying this to improve my quality of life, or merely because other people are buying it?"

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican North Carolina Rep. Chuck Edwards implored House colleagues to reconsider an Ethics Committee report that found he engaged in persistent, unprofessional and inappropriate conduct toward two female aides and recommended his censure.

Edwards' letter asks representatives to distinguish between unconventional conduct and sexual harassment.

"An affectionate friendship is not a sexual proposition. A gift is not sexual misconduct," he wrote. "A compliment is not sexual misconduct. Poetry is not sexual misconduct."

Edwards' letter, dated Tuesday, was first reported by the news outlet NOTUS.

The Ethics Committee on Thursday declined to comment in response to Edwards' letter.

The committee's report, which came nearly three months after it announced it was investigating Edwards, found that both women were uncomfortable with his behavior but found themselves in a difficult position because he was their boss and a member of Congress.

The report continued: "Rep. Edwards was at minimum blind to that reality, and at worst, dismissive of the impact his inappropriate conduct had on the careers and well-being of two women on his staff."

One aide worked for the congressman's office for about 2 1/2 years and the other for about three years. They no longer work there. The Ethics panel said the women left due to conduct described in its report, although they provided other explanations to Edwards at the time of their departures.

Edwards has denied that any of his conduct was intended as a sexual or romantic advance, but the committee said his behavior would "lead a reasonable observer to interpret it as such."

It also described his actions as "beyond inappropriate."

The report detailed numerous gifts that Edwards gave the two aides, calling the gifts "beyond norms of professional behavior." The women received jewelry totaling more than $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cellphone, as well as vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.

The committee earlier this month recommended censure, which registers the House's deep disapproval of a lawmaker's conduct that doesn't meet the threshold for expulsion.

Edwards, who was elected in 2022, dropped his reelection bid two days after the committee recommended he be censured.

The committee's investigation came at a time of heightened scrutiny of lawmakers' behavior toward female staffers following the resignations of Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell and Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales. Both faced calls for their expulsion before they stepped down.

title: AOC’s socialist credentials face fresh scrutiny after glaring 7-year gap surfaces: ‘Very convenient’

fullText:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez renewed her membership with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) following a seven-year lapse as the organization's national profile grows.

The New York congresswoman, widely viewed as a potential 2028 presidential contender, rejoined DSA this month as the group builds momentum from a string of Democratic primary victories, including over several incumbents. Although Ocasio-Cortez's formal membership had lapsed for seven years, she remained closely aligned with DSA, which continued to praise her and refer to her as a member.

"Democratic Socialists of America confirms Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a member in good standing of our organization, having recently rejoined in August 2026," DSA wrote in a statement shared with City & State New York, a local news outlet. "Previously, the representative joined DSA in 2018 with a one-year membership, which DSA's national leadership recently noticed had lapsed, in 2019. She has since renewed her membership as of this month."

2028 Battleground Poll Scrambles Democrats' Future As Insurgent Socialist Seizes Lead

DSA discovered the lapse after Ocasio-Cortez recently described herself as a member of its New York City chapter but not the national organization, prompting DSA leaders to review her membership status, City & State reported.

When Ocasio-Cortez first joined DSA, annual memberships had to be manually renewed each year. The organization has since moved to automatic renewals.

"This is LOL in a gently humorous way rather than LOL in a mean way," Washington Post columnist Megan McArdle posted on X in response to the news. "Could definitely have happened to me."

title: 10 Shows Like 'Ride or Die' You Should Watch Next
description: Spies, assassins, and ladies in over their heads
fullText:
Octavia Spencer and Hannah Waddingham make for an unbeatable pairing in the Prime Video series Ride or Die, which sees Spencer as Debbie, the American wife of a British MP and Waddingham as Judith, her bestie who, it turns out, is also an elite and highly trained assassin. Good thing, too, as Debbie's marriage puts her in mortal danger pretty much from the outset. It's a rather impressively funny action thriller, and, though not all of these shows hit the same comedic beats, they all involve women who find themselves in way over their heads.

Beth, Ruby, and Annie (Christina Hendricks, Retta, and Mae Whitman, respectively) are three moms in suburban Michigan, and they are all having serious money troubles. They're not exactly criminal masterminds, so they concoct a scheme to rob the local grocery store to solve them—a store that just happens to serve as a front for a money-laundering operation. They make off with $500,000—but the gang leader whose money they unknowingly stole wants it back. Oh, and the store manager spotted one of their distinctive tattoos and is threatening blackmail. It's definitely not a sitcom, but it's a solid comedy-drama with a talented cast of characters who keep finding themselves in deeper and deeper trouble over the course of four seasons. Stream Good Girls on Netflix.

How to Get to Heaven From Belfast comes from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, though that earlier and justifiably beloved show will only moderately prepare you for the latest. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that their fourth bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't, a mixed blessing given that they all have life-ruining secrets that they were hoping to bury. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the maybe-murder, and find themselves in way over their heads and in a complex web of secrets and old vendettas, with murder and some impressive amounts of mayhem going on. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, and the show has a beating heart beneath the absolute chaos. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

This crime thriller is based on the 1987 Debra Winger/Theresa Russell movie Black Widow; where that film was a stylish but fairly by-the-numbers neo-noir, the show adds depth and layers to both women at the its core: Emmy Rossum is FBI Agent Alice Black and Lola Pettigrew is foil and serial killer Catherine Grace. In this version, Catherine is sicker, more sly, and also more interesting, especially once her motivations are made known. The two leads have earned some rave reviews, and, while far less comedic than Ride or Die, it offers up some similar thriller beats, albeit from a darker place. Stream Furious on Hulu.

If it's a lady assassin you're in the market for, Nikita is one of pop culture's finest: This is just the most recent riff on Luc Besson's 1990 film La Femme Nikita, having inspired three movies and two TV shows (the earlier Canadian series is also pretty good). This one stars Maggie Q as the title's Nikita—she was brought up, Black Widow-style, to be a perfect killing machine working on behalf of a mysterious U.S. government black ops "Division"—but she fell in love with a guy who the Division then executed, and now she's out for revenge. She's going to bring down her former masters, and she's got some help from an agent of her own: Alex (Lyndsy Fonseca), a young woman who Nikita rescued and who now serves as a very handy mole. Stream Nikita on Tubi.

Sandra Oh and Jodie Comer star as the two halves of television's great cat-and-mouse narratives with Oh as Eve Polastri, a bored MI5 analyst who becomes obsessed with hunting down the brutal, notorious assassin known only as Villanelle. It starts as a professional compulsion before it gets personal, and it soon becomes clear that the fascination goes both ways. This is a spy thriller more than an action comedy, but there's a light touch when it comes to the central, and completely entrancing, relationship. Stream Killing Eve on Paramount+.

Christina Applegate and Linda Cardellini make for another all-time great TV pairing in this dark comedy about a couple of women who become united in tragedy and lies. Applegate is Jen Harding, a realtor whose husband was killed in a hit-and-run incident; she's not dealing very well, and takes a bit of inspiration from Cardellini's Judy, who has maintained a cheery disposition following her fiancé Steve's death from a heart attack—easier to do given that Steve's actually alive. And then we discover that Judy has a storage unit with a car that looks suspiciously like the one that killed Jen's husband. That's all part of the first episode, and the show only gets wilder from there. Stream Dead to Me on Netflix.

With this German import, we have a Cold War-era spy thriller punctuated by moments of very dark (but very funny) comedy. Jella Haase stars as Kleo Straub, a ruthless East German Stasi assassin who was framed for treason a couple of years before the series kicks off in 1989, and who's now free to pursue brutal revenge. Sven Petzold (Dimitrij Schaad), meanwhile, is the hapless police officer who's linked Kleo to a murder he'd been investigating, and pursues her before discovering that he's in way over his head. Stream Kleo on Netflix.

This genre-bender has been something of a hit for Netflix—enough to have earned a second-season renewal. Keira Knightley stars as Helen Webb, wife of the Secretary of State for Defence of the UK, and a secret spy in the employ of the mercenary spy organization of the title. She learns from her handler (Sarah Lancashire) that her lover has been killed, thus potentially blowing her cover, but luckily, she has a hitman bestie (Ben Whislaw) to help her out. It's all deliberately pulpy, with a tongue-in-cheek self-awareness that lightens the tone. Stream Black Doves on Netflix.

This one is more spy-adjacent, starring Emma Thompson as hard-living, hard-drinking private investigator Zoë Boehm. She's hired by Ruth Wilson's Sarah Trafford, a married art restorer who nobody takes very seriously (including and especially her husband), even when she becomes invested in the fate of a young girl whose family is killed in a gas explosion (allegedly) down the street. The girl, whose parents were killed, disappears into the system, and no one really seems to care until Sarah hires Zoë and her husband to look into it. Turns out both women are in way over their heads, as the missing girl points to a much broader conspiracy. The show's villains are a bit cartoonishly distracting, but Thompson and Wilson are brilliantly paired, and their performances are more than worth the price of admission. Stream Down Cemetery Road on Apple TV.

Messy flight attendant Cassie Bowden (Kaley Cuoco) drinks too much, and isn't terribly particular about the men she sleeps with—both of which come to bite her when she wakes up in a Bangkok hotel room with a dead body, the guy's neck having been slashed. Clumsily attempting to conceal her part in whatever happened (she can't quite remember), she's quickly drawn into a larger conspiracy that goes well beyond just the one dead man. Her best friend Annie (Zosia Mamet) is a lawyer doing her best to help, but Cassie doesn't make it easy. Stream The Flight Attendant on HBO Max.

title: If You Loved 'Lost,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
description: If you miss the ultimate mystery-box series, check out this 1990 Tim Robbins flick.
fullText:
It’s been more than 15 years since Lost went off the air, ending a legendary run on broadcast television. Though the show could be frustratingly slow to reveal its secrets, it remains one of the best TV shows of the modern era—and one of the most influential, with a host of other series playing off a similar “mystery box” premise and shuffled timeline.

Fans of the show have never stopped looking for a viewing experience that matches it in terms of surprise and heartfelt, emotionally rich storytelling (if that describes you, you’ve probably already watched all of these streamalikes offering similar vibes), so allow me to suggest the one movie that fits the bill perfectly: Jacob’s Ladder, a 1990 psychological thriller starring Tim Robbins.

On the surface, Jacob’s Ladder might not seem like an immediate match for the heady sci-fi-tinged, character-based storytelling of Lost—but once you dig deeper, the narrative and tonal parallels become clear. In the film, Jacob Singer (Robbins) is a struggling Vietnam Veteran living in Brooklyn in 1975, four years after a disturbing incident with his unit that ended with Jacob being stabbed by a bayonet. Haunted by his dead son and his wartime experiences, Jacob’s descends into a living nightmare, filled with hallucinations of monstrous figures. But something most mysterious is happening, and while the ending is a clear antecedent to Lost’s infamous finale, there are many visual echoes as well.

Jacob’s Ladder is arguably a horror movie, and is certainly more frightening and disturbing than Lost, which was more philosophical and even optimistic in its approach. But the way Jacob’s reality is plagued by a mounting sense of mystery and dread will remind you a lot of the early seasons of Lost, when the Others and the Hatch were ominous mirages hiding in the shadows of that mysterious island. And the film's ultimate payoff—and its message that sometimes, the devils we perceive to be attacking us are actually angels trying to save us—will resonate with anyone who was all-in on Jack Shephard’s inner struggles (and Lost’s overarching themes of atonement and redemption).

Finally, there’s the non-linear way Jacob’s Ladder deals with time, which echoes the flashbacks, flash-forwards, and flash-sideways moments in Lost. As Jacob’s life dissolves into an increasingly hellish chaos, his experience of time becomes shuffled and blurred, with the past (and alternate futures) intruding on the present in disorienting ways. Just like in the show, these flashes of Jacob’s life slowly paint a picture of his true present, and his ultimate fate. It’s an intense and often frightening film, but fans of Lost will love it. Stream Jacob’s Ladder on Fubo or rent it on Prime Video.

Need more mysterious islands, heavy sci-fi concepts, and stories of survival against supernatural forces? Here are a few more movies for Lost fans.

Deserted island? Check. Mysterious monster? Check. Flawed people hiding secrets? Check. When her boat sinks, Jenn (Kiersey Clemons) washes ashore on an island where the only sign of humanity is a set of old graves. At night, she’s attacked by a terrifying sea monster. When some of her friends wash up on the beach, having also survived the disaster, they don’t believe Jenn's warnings—and shebegins to wonder if she can trust them. If you loved the survival aspect of Lost’s story combined with the complex (and often hidden) relationships between the characters, Sweetheart will go down easy. Rent Sweetheart on Prime Video.

If you want more stories about a group of strangers who find themselves in an isolated and ominous wilderness, with a puzzle box mystery that has to be pieced together, this 2014 adaptation of the novel by James Dashner is the ticket. Waking up without any memory, teenage Thomas finds himself in the Glade, where the only possible escape is through a dense maze surrounding it. The maze is patrolled by dangerous biomechanical creatures called Grievers. Determined to escape, Thomas and a group of other imprisoned teens must acquire clues to the maze’s operation and eventually learn what’s really going on. Like on Lost, it involves a mysterious organization, seemingly abandoned facilities, and a mounting series of twists. Rent The Maze Runner on Prime Video.

Part of what hooked people on Lost was just the basic premise—a group of strangers crash-land on an island and have to figure out how to survive. The Beach isn’t a mystery, but it leans into those very human dynamics as a group of young travelers (led by a baby Leonardo DiCaprio) find their way to a pristine, isolated beach where a group of people has established an ersatz community focused on keeping the idyllic place a secret. The "Others" here are the drug dealers who tolerate the group near their farms—for now—while the biggest risk may be the slow breakdown of order among the islanders themselves. If your favorite parts of Lost involved the factions forming among the survivors, the Tailies, and the Others, watch this movie. Rent The Beach on Prime Video.

https://www.amazon.com/Beach-Leonardo-DiCaprio/dp/B000I9X6BS

Lost probably sucked you in with the hints of mystery amid the human drama generated by a group of plane crash survivors with a lot of secrets, but it slowly evolved into a sci-fi show involving time travel and a lot of other speculative stuff. If you want to break your brain with a complex time travel story that pivots off of flawed humanity and emotionally-driven bad decisions, watch Primer: When two engineers stumble upon a limited way to travel backward in time, they begin experimenting—but when, exactly, the experiments started, and which version of the character you’re watching at any given time, soon becomes a complex puzzle (seriously, there are charts online trying to figure it all out). Rent Primer on Prime Video.

The Village got some hate when it was released, but if you love the eerie atmosphere and shocking reveals of Lost, this M. Night Shyamalan joint is a great match. In an isolated 19th-century village, residents keep strict watch for unnamed monsters that lurk in the surrounding woods. When one of the villagers is grievously wounded, blind Ivy (Bryce Dallas Howard) enters the woods on a quest to travel to the wicked, forbidden “towns” to retrieve medicine. A series of reveals lets the audience in on the secrets of the insular community in classic Shyamalan fashion, and the origins of the settlement echo the founding of the DHARMA Initiative in ways that Lost fans will appreciate. Rent The Village on Prime Video.

title: Evbuomwan impresses as GB cruise past Switzerland

fullText:
Great Britain started their pre-qualifying campaign for 2029 EuroBasket with a convincing 110-75 win over Switzerland in Fribourg.

Boston Celtics centre Amari Williams and Barcelona forward Tosan Evbuomwan both made their debuts for Great Britain's senior side in the victory to put GB top of Group E.

Evbuomwan, who spent three years in the NBA, making 50 appearances prior to his move to Barcelona earlier this summer, contributed 21points in 25 minutes.

His added NBA quality alongside Williams, who has just finished his first season with the Celtics, allowed GB to claim an impressive win.

Williams posted eight points and seven rebounds in 19 minutes, while Josh Uduje top scored with 24 points for the visitors.

Marc Steutel's side were comfortable from the off in their first competitive match since missing out on qualifying for the 2027 Fiba World Cup.

Great Britain won each of the four quarters, taking the opening two by six points each.

Ranked 45th in the world with their opponents 16 places below them, Great Britain cemented their dominance after half-time to lead 79-51 at the end of the third quarter.

With one eye on Sunday's match against Slovakia in Newcastle, Evbuomwan and Williams were among those afforded some rest time in the fourth quarter.

title: Ukraine file complaint over FIA lifting Russia ban
description: The Ukrainian Automobile Federation requests an urgent investigation into its Russian counterpart, the RAF.
fullText:
Ukraine has lodged a formal complaint with the ethics committee of motorsport's governing body the FIA following the decision to lift the ban on Russian competitors in international events.

The Ukrainian Automobile Federation (FAU) has requested an urgent investigation into its Russian counterpart, the RAF.

The ban on individuals from Russia and Belarus competing in international motorsport events had been in place since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The move was approved by the FIA world council, to which sources have told BBC Sport it was proposed by FIA president Mohammed ben Sulayem.

The FAU says the Russian Automobile Federation has "opened and continues to operate" offices in regions of Ukraine occupied by Russia - Crimea, the city of Sevastopol and the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia Oblasts.

These are recognised by the United Nations as sovereign Ukrainian territory.

The FAU says these actions are in breach of both the FIA statutes and its international sporting code, which permit only one automobile club per country.

FAU president Oleksandr Feldman said: "This is a clear breach of the FIA statutes by the Russian Automobile Federation, which, as an FIA member organisation, is bound to comply with them.

"We urge the FIA president to take urgent action to have these offices closed, and for the Russian automobile federation to be sanctioned for its actions."

The Ukrainian club has requested the FIA ethics committee find the RAF in breach of FIA statutes and order it to close the offices with immediate effect.

The statement also points out that the head of the RAF, Boris Rotenberg, is "directly subject to international sanctions imposed by the US, UK, EU, and other allied jurisdictions in response to aggression against Ukraine".

The decision to lift the ban on Russian and Belarusian competitors followed a similar move by the International Olympic Association.

Following changes to the FIA statutes last year, the FIA ethics committee is under the control of Ben Sulayem and his ally the president of the senate, Carmelo Sanz de Barros.

The FIA has been approached for comment.

title: Pogacar fights off Mas challenge to win stage six
description: Tadej Pogacar recovers from a brief off-road excursion to claim his third victory at the Vuelta a Espana but he is made to fight all the way to the line by Enric Mas.
fullText:
Tadej Pogacar recovered from a brief off-road excursion to outsprint Enric Mas and claim his third victory at this year's Vuelta a Espana, but he was made to fight all the way to the line by the Spaniard on stage six.

After attacking on the final climb and rapidly establishing a handsome lead it looked as though the defending world champion would romp away to a trademark solo victory.

But, as the rest of the main contenders struggled in his slipstream, Movistar's Mas reeled him in and overtook him on the final metres of the climb to claim maximum points in the king of the mountain's classification.

The home rider then initially led down the final descent, at one point gesturing to Pogacar to take it cautiously.

But the six-time Grand Tour winner, who is chasing the Vuelta crown to complete the set with victory in all three of the sport's biggest stage races, having already won five Tours de France and a Giro d'Italia, did not heed the warning.

He skipped past Mas on the inside at a corner and soon put distance between them, only to overcook it on the next corner and go into the small rocks at the side of the Tarmac.

His excellent bike-handling skills enabled him to scrub off enough speed to prevent a serious crash and he was soon on his way again, but he was content to follow Mas down the rest of the descent before the pair worked together to put time into the chasers, with Pogacar's superior sprint securing him yet another stage win in his already glittering career.

The result means the 27-year-old's lead in the general classification now stands at three minutes and 34 seconds, with Mas climbing to second overall.

Meanwhile, Welsh rider Josh Tarling, whose brother Finlay died two weeks ago at the age of 19 after a collision with a vehicle in the Tour of Portugal, abandoned the race with about 120km remaining.

"Josh Tarling's brave La Vuelta has come to an end and he's decided to stop. We couldn't be prouder," said his team Netcompany Ineos on social media.

Tarling produced a strong performance in the opening stage, coming third behind Pogacar and Ethan Hayter in an individual time trial.

After the stage, Pogacar said he was "really surprised" by how Mas passed him "like a rocket" at the summit.

"I was not expecting it because I heard on the radio I was 40 seconds ahead of the chasers and Enric wasn't mentioned," he said.

"When he passed me, I was little bit shocked. I was sure he knew the downhill and I was happy to be with [him] for the last 10 km with headwind.

"I knew I could beat [him] in the sprint. I appreciated that he committed fully, and I also committed fully to the line. It was a good race."

While Pogacar has now won half the stages so far in this edition of the Vuelta, Mas' performance provided the home crowd with plenty to cheer, as he jumped above four-time winner Primoz Roglic in the GC race.

Roglic finished 46 seconds back in a group with Ramses Debruyne, Richard Carapaz and Felix Gall.

It was a bad day for Briton Oscar Onley, who lost over a minute-and-a-half to the winner.

On Friday, the peloton will take a mountainous 149.8km route from Vall d'Alba to Aramon Valdelinares.

title: Durham will pick bowler Carse until told otherwise
description: Durham coach Ryan Campbell says he is comfortable with selecting Brydon Carse, and will continue to do so unless they are told otherwise.
fullText:
Durham coach Ryan Campbell says he is comfortable with continuing to select England bowler Brydon Carse, and says the club will continue to do so unless they are told otherwise.

Carse, 31, was briefly arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly after Durham's win over Derbyshire on Saturday, with images on social media showing Carse in handcuffs and surrounded by police officers.

He was removed from England's squad for the second Test against Pakistan after the Cricket Regulator began an investigation, but Durham picked him on Thursday for their County Championship match against Gloucestershire.

"He feels he's let the group down," Campbell told BBC Sport.

"The England team are trying to restart their whole way of going about it and he feels he's let them down.

"At the end of the day, he will have to live with that.

"I'm not going to stand here and say I've never made a mistake but what we can do is get our arms around him and make sure he doesn't make those mistakes again."

On Monday, Derbyshire Police said a man had been briefly detained outside Molly Malone's bar before being de-arrested.

They say they are looking into allegations of assault and their investigation remains ongoing.

Carse, who has 58 England caps, appears unlikely to be selected by the national team until the regulator completes its investigation. That process will be delayed by the police probe.

"[The regulator] is going to do their job, we're going to listen to what they say," Campbell said.

"When they give us a result, we'll act accordingly.

"Until then, everyone is free to play, he's free to play for Durham, and he'll continue to play."

The incident is the latest in a line of off-field issues involving players from England's men's team.

Carse's Durham team-mate Ben Stokes, the former England captain, was left out for a Test after breaking the team's midnight curfew earlier this year.

Asked if circumstances would require Durham to take a harder line with a player, Campbell said: "So far, I've never had to deal with that, so let's hope I don't have to deal with that."

Carse took a wicket in his first over against Gloucestershire and finished with figures of 2-51 from 12 overs as Division Two's bottom side were dismissed for 137.

title: Wigan thrash Hull KR on night of tributes for Boston
description: Wigan Warriors move top of Super League as they thrash Hull KR on an emotional evening as the Cherry and Whites pay tribute to the late Sir Billy Boston.
fullText:
Tries: Marshall 3, Field, Eckersley 2, Keighran, Wardle Goals: Keighran 7

Wigan Warriors moved top of Super League as they thrashed Hull KR on an emotional evening as the Cherry and Whites paid tribute to the late Sir Billy Boston.

The rugby league great, who scored a remarkable 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan and helped them win three Challenge Cups and the Championship during his time with the club, died this week at the age of 92.

Liam Marshall scored a hat-trick of tries as Jai Field, Zach Eckersley, Adam Keighran and Jake Wardle all got on the scoresheet in a decent night's work for the hosts.

It was a difficult evening for the visitors who, other than Frankie Dearlove having a second-half try chalked off, offered little in trying conditions with torrential rain making an impact on the playing surface for the second half.

Victory for Wigan means they move two points clear of Leeds Rhinos, while Hull KR remain in sixth and head into their final two games of the regular season two points clear of St Helens in pursuit of the final play-off spot.

A Great Britain international and World Cup winner, Boston was the first black British player to play in Australia and New Zealand when he joined the Great Britain side which toured there in 1954.

Last year, Boston became the first player in rugby league's 130-year history to receive a knighthood.

Wreaths were laid and a rendition of Jerusalem was sung in the lead-up to kick-off in tribute to Boston as both sides paid their respects.

Wigan, who wore "Billy" on the front of their shirts thanks to an agreement with their primary sponsor,, external did not take long to get going against Hull KR.

Boston: The winger who rewrote rugby league's record books

Marshall got Wigan going after nine minutes when he collected Harry Smith's high kick to the corner and another Smith kick soon after sent Field away to score his 100th career try.

Eckersley went in shortly after as Wigan gained ground courtesy of Smith's pinpoint 40/20 kick and he scored his second try just before the half-hour mark after a frantic period in which the hosts somehow kept their attack alive and worked it wide for him to run in at the corner.

Before the first half was out, Marshall put in an acrobatic dive to dot down and Keighran got the second half going.

The Robins fielded a depleted side, with only eight of the 17 from last week's loss to Toulouse featuring in the trip to the Brick Community Stadium, with Jez Litten, Tom Davies and Peta Hiku rested, while Mikey Lewis and Tevita Pangai Jr were still suspended.

It was a shift from earlier this season when Wigan named a heavily rotated and youthful side in a 62-4 defeat in a Super League game, before the two sides met again at Wembley in the Challenge Cup final nine days later.

Dearlove thought he had scored on his KR debut when he slid to the line on a pitch still holding water after an earlier downpour, but his try was chalked off after Bevan French put in an incredible defensive effort to hold the ball up before the young centre could ground it.

Marshall then brought up his hat-trick with relative ease as the game closed out and Wardle put the gloss on a win which means that Leeds, with their vastly superior points difference, will have to beat St Helens on Friday to regain top spot.

Wigan Warriors boss Matt Peet told BBC Radio Manchester:

"It was a fitting occasion for Billy with everything the club did and the atmosphere in the ground.

"I thought the performance was befitting.

"The fans and the people in the crowd who've had a sad week, we have a responsibility."

Hull KR head coach Willie Peters told BBC Radio Humberside:

"I'm really proud of the performance. We had a young side tonight and we didn't stop fighting until the end. We played against a good team, who were extremely disciplined and give you nothing.

"The inexperience we had in this team tonight, the main thing is that we said we need to fight for everything. We gave them a few things but they did the badge proud.

"I've always said players have to earn the jersey, it's not given to them. It was different circumstances tonight and there were probably three players who could have played but they've played a lot of rugby league."

title: Ipswich sign Argentina World Cup winner Palacios
description: Argentina midfielder Exequiel Palacios becomes the first World Cup winner to sign for Ipswich Town after joining from Bayer Leverkusen.
fullText:
Argentina midfielder Exequiel Palacios has become the first World Cup winner to sign for Ipswich Town after joining from Bayer Leverkusen.

Palacios, 27, left the Bundesliga club for an undisclosed fee and has signed a four-year contract with the Premier League newcomers.

He was part of the Argentina side that both won the World Cup in 2022 and reached the final this summer while he also won the Copa America twice with his country.

"This is a club with great ambition and I am excited to play football in England and compete against some of the best clubs and players in the world," Palacios said.

Palacios, Ipswich's 11th signing of the transfer window, started Argentina's 3-1 win against World Cup debutants Jordan in the group stage in his only appearance at the 2026 tournament.

Ipswich manager Gary O'Neil added: "He is a player who has had real success at the top level of the game, winning the biggest prize of all in the World Cup, as well as major trophies at club level.

"That experience will be vital for us as we continue to work to improve the squad this summer."

Palacios made his senior debut for his boyhood club River Plate in 2015 and won the Copa Libertadores in 2018 and the Copa Argentina twice.

He moved to Germany in 2020 and made 24 appearances as Leverkusen claimed their first-ever Bundesliga title in 2023-24.

Under current Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso, he also won the DFB Pokal and the German Super Cup during his six years at the BayArena.

He departs Leverkusen after making 186 appearances and scoring 15 goals.

Ipswich have spent more than £150m since returning to the Premier League and are also progressing with a move to sign Tammy Abraham on loan from Aston Villa.

They made a winning return to the top flight, defeating Sunderland 2-1 at Portman Road and have also reached the third round of the Carabao Cup at the expense of League One Leicester City.

title: Fleetwood in contention as Lee leads Tour Championship
description: Defending champion Tommy Fleetwood shoots a four-under 66 to put himself in contention at the Tour Championship at East Lake in Atlanta.
fullText:
Tour Championship - first round

-8 MW Lee (Aus); -6 V Hovland (Nor), C Morikawa (US), C Gotterup (US); -5 R Gerard (US), A Bhatia (US), L Aberg (Swe), S Scheffler (US)

Selected others: -4 T Fleetwood (Eng), M Fitzpatrick (Eng), R Fox (NZ); -3 R MacIntyre (Sco), W Clark (US); -2 J Rose (Eng), A Fitzpatrick (Eng), R McIlroy (NI)

Defending champion Tommy Fleetwood shot a four-under 66 to put himself in contention, four strokes off first-round leader Min Woo Lee at the Tour Championship in Atlanta.

However, Northern Ireland's Rory McIlroy endured a mixed start in his bid to win a record-extending fourth Fedex Cup, bogeying two of the first four holes before fighting back on the back nine to sign for a 68.

Lee, who won last month's Scottish Open, carded a bogey-free 62 to set the pace at eight under as he equalled his best ever round on the PGA Tour in its season-ending event at East Lake.

Australia's Lee is two strokes clear of Norway's Viktor Hovland, who triumphed in 2023, and American duo Collin Morikawa and Chris Gotterup.

It was a fine display from Lee, who was second from last in the BMW Championship a week ago and found himself without a partner for most of the day, with JJ Spaun withdrawing through injury after four holes.

"It was a little strange at first, just like looking for a playing partner and you're just there by yourself," said Lee.

"It was more just maintaining speeds and not rushing because I would just catch the group in front and wait. So I had to just slow down a little bit. It worked out."

Ominously, world number one Scottie Scheffler ended his round with a birdie on the 18th to sit at five under, with England's Matt Fitzpatrick in the mix at four under after also making a birdie four on the concluding hole.

Scotland's Robert MacIntyre is at three under, with the highlight of his day arriving on the sixth hole when he rolled in a putt from over 30 feet for an eagle.

England's Justin Rose and Alex Fitzpatrick both signed for rounds of 68 on a day when none of the 29 players in the field to complete the round went over par.

The winner on Sunday will take home the Fedex Cup and a $10m (£7.4m) prize.

title: Man City and Aston Villa to face holders PSG in Champions League
description: European champions Paris St-Germain will face Premier League duo Manchester City and Aston Villa in the league phase of this season's Champions League.
fullText:
European champions Paris St-Germain will face Premier League duo Manchester City and Aston Villa as well as five-time winners Barcelona in the league phase of this season's Champions League.

The back-to-back Champions League winners will welcome Barca to Parc des Princes, while they were also handed trips to Villa Park and Manchester in the draw for the league phase.

Premier League champions Arsenal, meanwhile, will host 15-time winners Real Madrid at Emirates Stadium, and have also been handed a trip to Bayern Munich.

Mikel Arteta's men, who were beaten by PSG on penalties in the final last season, will face Borussia Dortmund, Real Betis, Lille, Napoli, Azerbaijan champions Sabah and Slavia Prague as well.

Enzo Maresca's City will welcome PSG to Etihad Stadium and travel to Barcelona, where they will have a reunion with Spanish World Cup-winner Rodri, who moved to the Nou Camp in a £65m deal this summer.

City will also be up against another of their former midfielders in Kevin de Bruyne when Napoli visit Manchester, with Sporting, Porto, RB Leipzig, AEK Athens and Lens their other opponents.

Europa League winners Villa, returning to the competition after a season away, will host PSG and Dortmund and travel to Barcelona and Galatasaray.

Unai Emery's side also face Club Brugge, Fenerbahce, Viking and Slavia Prague.

Manchester United, returning after a two-year hiatus, will meet Bayern, Atletico Madrid, Roma, Sporting, Leipzig, Villarreal, Sabah and Como.

Liverpool, meanwhile, host Atletico, Porto, Villarreal and Lens while visiting Inter Milan, Brugge, Fenerbahce and LASK.

The first league-phase matches will be played on Tuesday, 8 September and the last round of games will take place on 27 January 2027, with the exact schedule to be released on Saturday.

This season's final will be held in Madrid on 5 June.

Arsenal: Real Madrid (home), Bayern Munich (away), Borussia Dortmund (home), Real Betis (away), Lille (home), Napoli (away), Sabah (home), Slavia Prague (away)

Aston Villa: PSG (home), Barcelona (away), Borussia Dortmund (home), Club Brugge (away), Fenerbahce (home), Galatasaray (away), Viking (home), Slavia Prague (away)

Liverpool: Atletico Madrid (home), Inter Milan (away), Porto (home), Club Brugge (away), Villarreal (home), Fenerbahce (away), Lens (home), LASK (away)

Manchester City: PSG (home), Barcelona (away), Sporting Club (home), Porto (away), Napoli (home), Leipzig (away), AEK Athens (home), Lens (away)

Manchester United: Bayern Munich (home), Atletico Madrid (away), Roma (home), Sporting Club (away), Leipzig (home), Villarreal (away), Sabah (home), Como (away)

Each of the 36 teams plays eight different teams - four at home and four away - in the league phase.

Teams who finish in the top eight automatically qualify for the last 16, while those placing ninth to 24th will compete in a two-legged knockout play-off for the chance to join them.

Sides who finish 25th or lower will be eliminated, and will not drop into the Europa League.

Last season, eventual runners-up Arsenal topped the league phase standings with 24 points after eight wins from as many matches.

Liverpool were third - behind second-placed Bayern Munich - with 18 points while Tottenham finished one point behind in fourth.

Chelsea and Manchester City also qualified directly for the last 16 after finishing sixth and eighth respectively while Newcastle finished 12th.

Chelsea, Manchester City, Newcastle and Spurs were knocked out in the last 16 last season while Liverpool were beaten in the quarter-finals by PSG, who also edged Arsenal in the final for their second consecutive title.

title: Werro edges closer to 800m mark as world records fall in Zurich
description: European champion Audrey Werro came tantalisingly close to downing the oldest outdoor world record in athletics, finishing a little more than four tenths of a second off Jarmila Kratochvilova's 800m mark.
fullText:
European champion Audrey Werro came tantalisingly close to downing the oldest outdoor world record in athletics, finishing a little more than four tenths of a second off Jarmila Kratochvilova's 800m mark of one minute 53.28 seconds, set 43 years ago.

Roared on by a 25,000-strong capacity crowd at the Zurich Diamond League, the Swiss hit the final 100m almost in stride with the infield pacing lights which had been set for a world record.

However Werro, straining hard against the clock, could not quite find the finishing pace she needed, clocking 1:53.70.

Still, the third-fastest time in history shaves another tenth of a second off the 22-year-old's personal best and only increases the sense that she will break the record sooner rather than later.

"As far as the world record is concerned, I saw the light, but there was a lot of movement during the race and it was not calm," said Werro, who caused second-placed Femke Broeders-Bol to check as she overtook the Dutchwoman at the start of her kick for home on the back straight.

"I still had enough energy at the end of the race to accelerate and to stay in the lead. Yes, it was tight for the world record, it was not meant for today.

"I am so proud to be able to run those sub-1:54 times, which shows that I can run consistently and fast now and this is good for the future."

Werro has improved every year of her top-level career and now, having finished her studies and concentrating on the track, has shown ruthless consistency. She has four of the top-10 all-time 800m times, all clocked this summer.

For Britain's Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson, who withdrew from the meeting after her exertions in taking continental silver behind Werro in Birmingham, it only emphasised the challenge she faces in the event.

Not only does she have to contend with Werro's burgeoning form, but Broeders-Bol, the world 400m hurdles champion who has switched up to two laps this season, gave another impressive showing in her debut campaign over 800m.

The Dutchwoman, who took out the pace initially, clocked a new national record of 1:54.71, beating Hodgkinson's training partner and Commonwealth 800m champion Georgia Hunter-Bell, who finished in 1:55.03, into third.

Broeders-Bol's long, languid stride and sprint speed have already made an impression in the event and she is gaining tactical knowhow fast as she acclimatises to the bump and hustle of middle distance.

"I was hoping to be in these sort of fights, but to be honest, I didn't expect it at all in the first season," she said afterwards.

"I thought I needed at least one or two seasons to get into the 1:54s, but here I am."

When Athing Mu-Nikolayev, Hodgkinson's American nemesis who beat her to gold at the Tokyo Olympics and Eugene 2022, slipped off the scene, the Briton had hoped to dominate the 800m.

With less than two years until she defends her Olympic crown in Los Angeles however, new rivals are looking ever more threatening.

Hodgkinson, like Werro and Broeders-Bol, has qualified for the Diamond League final in Brussels on 4-5 September. It could be an intriguing benchmark for the season's end.

While Werro fell short in her world record attempt, two new marks were set in an astonishng night of action.

First, Brazil's Alison dos Santos defied expectations to smash the 400m hurdles world record.

The 26-year-old has been in excellent form this season, undefeated in the event, but there was little to suggest that Karsten Warholm's 2021 mark of 45.94 seconds was in danger.

But, with Warholm a distant second, Tokyo 2025 silver medallist Dos Santos cantered off the final hurdle and pushed through to clock 45.80 seconds.

His previous personal best stood at 46.29 and was set four years ago.

Just 75 minutes later, another world record fell in front of the 25,000-strong capacity crowd

Masai Russell, the Olympic champion, capturing the 100m hurdles mark was less surprising, considering the American has finished within a tenth of a second of Tobi Amusan's 12.12-second landmark five times in the past two seasons.

The 26-year-old celebrated her 12.09 clocking with a finger to her lips as the crowd erupted. Just like Warholm, Amusan had a prime view of her record being broken, finishing second.

Amy Hunt, winner of four golds at the European Championships earlier this month, found things tougher against some of the world's finest 100m runners.

Left in the blocks, the Briton had to watch on as Olympic champion Julien Alfred inflicted Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's first defeat over the distance in two years, edging out the American in a 10.70-second photo finish.

David Rudisha's 800m world record of one minute 40.91 seconds, set en route to gold at London 2012, survived unscathed as his Kenyan compatriot Emmanuel Wanyonyi came home in one minute 41.76 seconds.

While Sweden's Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis, pushed on by competition from Greece's Emmanouil Karalis, failed in three shots at improving his own pole vault world record to 6.32m.

Jakob Ingebrigtsen, who has been booked in for a keenly-anticipated duel with Britain's Josh Kerr at the inaugural Ultimate Championships on 11-13 September, could only finish fifth in a 1500m race won by American Olympic champion Cole Hocker.

title: Smith & Cox help England to 248-9 on truncated day one
description: Jamie Smith and Jordan Cox battle difficult conditions and an improved Pakistan performance to take England to a competitive total on the opening day of the second Test.
fullText:
Second Rothesay Test, Lord's (day one of five)

England 248-9: Smith 61, Cox 55; Abbas 4-56

Jamie Smith and Jordan Cox battled difficult conditions and an improved Pakistan performance to take England to a competitive total on the opening day of the second Test.

In the damp and gloom at Lord's, Smith made 61 and Cox 55 to take England to 248-9 on a first day that was delayed by rain and curtailed by bad light.

The value of the hosts' score will only be revealed in time. The Lord's pitch is much better than the poor surface used for England's win against New Zealand in June, while more rain is forecast for the next three days.

It could be that England have batted themselves into a position from where they can win this match and the series, which would be a successful end to a troubling week dominated by the Brydon Carse controversy.

Cox was again impressive in only his third Test. He added 67 for the sixth wicket with Smith, who looked fluent for a much-needed half-century.

England were boosted by a late cameo of 34 not out from Gus Atkinson, while Pakistan were led by four wickets from Muhammad Abbas and three from Mohammad Ali. Things could have better for the tourists had they not dropped three catches.

Under a dark sky and with the floodlights on, England would probably have wanted to bowl before the day was out, only for the light to end proceedings.

England close on 248-9 against Pakistan - day one as it happened

Durham will pick bowler Carse until told otherwise

TMS podcast: Abbas masterclass as Smith stars on day one

For England, the chance to win their first Test series since 2024 comes after yet another off-field drinking incident.

Carse was removed from the squad for this Test after a night out in Derby on Saturday, with police investigating allegations of an assault. Carse is in the Durham side for their ongoing County Championship match against Gloucestershire.

The home side steamrollered Pakistan at Headingley in Joe Root's first Test back as captain. It was always likely Pakistan would improve on their performance from Leeds, simply because the tourists could not play much worse.

Pakistan were boosted by the return of captain Babar Azam from a hand injury, in the side for Salman Ali Agha who skippered in Leeds. Babar's first impact was to call correctly and play finally got under way at 12:20 BST.

The tourists' trio of fast-medium seamers were ideally suited to the conditions and they showed much greater control than last week.

England were sometimes wasteful - Dan Lawrence ran himself out and Harry Brook was bowled driving - and sometimes unlucky - Emilio Gay was caught down the leg side. For the most part, the batters were happy to roll up their sleeves, another encouraging sign early in Root's second reign.

The result was a compelling contest, an arm wrestle with neither side ever able to claim they held the upper hand.

England's total seems at least workable, yet Pakistan have the chance to gain a foothold if they bat well. This could turn into a tight Test.

Cox is already showing himself to be difficult to leave out once Jacob Bethell returns from a knee injury, and one way England could retain him would be as wicketkeeper ahead of Smith.

On this occasion, they combined for the two telling batting contributions of the day, albeit in contrasting styles.

Abbas did the damage to the top order, with Root once again lbw with the keeper up to the stumps. When Lawrence was run out in a mix-up with Cox, England were 120-5 and teetering.

Smith was given a life on 15 when keeper Muhammad Rizwan completely missed an edge off Ali. Reprieved, he dominated the strike and scoring in the stand with Cox, forcing the ball through the covers and whipping off his pads.

It took a moment of magic to part them. Salman, on as a sub, flew to his right at second slip to hold Cox, one-handed, off Khurram Shahzad.

This was an opportunity for Pakistan to get back into the series. Had England won the toss it feels reasonable to suspect the home bowlers would have made life very difficult for the fragile visiting batting.

Abbas was magnificent. At one point he claimed three wickets for four runs in the space of 16 balls - Gay, Ben Duckett and Root.

He received support from Ali, whose three wickets were all batters bowled by the ball nipping down the Lord's slope. Brook, Smith and Ollie Robinson were his victims.

Two of Pakistan's drops did not prove too costly. Root was missed at third slip by Imam-ul-Haq on one, though the skipper was out for four. Shan Masood spilled a simple catch at mid-wicket when Lawrence had 10, then the same fielder made amends to run out Lawrence for 17.

Rizwan's miss was the most costly, symptomatic of the keeper and slip fielders appearing to stand too deep for most of the day with a number of edges not carrying through.

title: 'Mortified' McInnes takes responsibility for Rangers' European exit
description: Manager Derek McInnes says he takes "full responsibility" for Rangers' "embarrassing" Conference League exit at the hands of Jablonec.
fullText:
Manager Derek McInnes says he takes "full responsibility" for Rangers' "embarrassing" Conference League exit at the hands of Jablonec.

Rangers, who held a 1-0 lead going into the second leg of the play-off in Czech Republic, lost 4-3 on penalties on Thursday to crash out of Europe completely.

Derek McInnes' side actually led early in the shootout, only for Findlay Curtis and James Penrice to miss their final two penalties.

It leaves them without European football beyond August for the first time since the 2-1 aggregate defeat by Luxembourg's Progres Niederkorn in the Europa League first qualifying round in 2017.

Have expensively-assembled Rangers improved at all under McInnes?

Latest Rangers news, analysis and fan views

And it ratchets up the pressure on McInnes after a hapless start to his reign at Ibrox, which included a Europa League exit against Jagiellonia Bialystok and a draw and defeat in their opening two Premiership games.

"I'm embarrassed with the performance," the Rangers manager said.

"The only people who represented the club well tonight were my staff and the supporters who were outstanding, getting behind the team despite watching what we all watched.

"I'm not going to make any excuses. Yes there's been a big turnover of players, yes we looked inexperienced at times but the responsibility is mine to make sure we're better than what we served up tonight.

"We're elite in everything we do in terms of preparation and the performance lacked in everything."

The stats back up McInnes' anger. Rangers had just over 46% possession during the 120 minutes in the Czech Republic, and just one shot on target.

They won fewer than 70% of their 16 tackles and committed 17 fouls.

"I can't accept, and we shouldn't accept, losing individual battles, duels, second balls, not winning enough tackles and just getting the momentum of the game going our way," the former Hearts manager added.

"I thought we looked young, inexperienced at times. We're trying to make some signings to help with that side of it but we need to do so much more as a team.

"We got what we deserved. If we'd won on penalties we would have taken it, of course, but it would only have covered over the cracks.

"I'm mortified with the performance. I know you can lose games of football but we should have enough in the building to take care of that tonight."

Rangers had won their two previous games - a 5-1 win over St Mirren in the League Cup and the 1-0 victory against Jablonec at Ibrox - after drawing at Dundee United and losing at home to Hibernian in their opening two Premiership matches.

But McInnes - who confirmed that no bid has yet been received for the absent Nico Raskin - feels this latest result may set them back.

"We went into this game scrambling for some sort of confidence, some positivity," he said. "But I just thought the team that deserved to go through went through tonight and that's hard for me to take."

Former Rangers midfielder Andy Halliday: "Rangers had no style, no desire, no movement, no tackles, no shots, no control. They offered absolutely nothing over 120 minutes. I'm not that shocked given what I've watched in the first few games.

"The questions are going to start coming Derek McInnes' way. Rangers played five different formations tonight and they offered nothing.

"They had a week to prepare for this game. I don't know what they did. I didn't see how they were going to score. They got played through far too easy.

"I think of Kaunas, Progres Niederkorn - that's up there with those defeats. This is one of the worst results in Rangers' recent history."

Former Rangers striker Steven Thompson: "One shot on target in 120 minutes. That tells a story about Rangers' threat.

"When players are on the pitch and things aren't going well and they look around them for someone to grab the game by the scruff of the neck, to lead, there's no answers.

"I could see Derek's frustration. He couldn't believe what he was watching. He tried numerous different things to bring about a better level of performance. But they need better quality on the pitch - and they need a gameplan."

BBC Scotland chief sportswriter Tom English: "They were passive and there was no get up and go about any of them. In a properly-functioning team, which this clearly is not, there would be one or two in there who, out of pure anger at their haplessness, would try and get something going but there was nobody.

"There was nobody out there berating, cajoling, encouraging, there was none of that. They all just went down with the ship. It didn't matter what Derek McInnes did, nobody responded.

"McInnes will be looking at this thinking they've put a lot of work into it, spent a lot of money, tried a lot of formations and nothing is working. What does he do now?"

Barry: Rangers are kidding themselves on. They are nowhere near the level they think they are, mediocre players, inexperienced staff, incompetent board. Be lucky to finish top six this season.

Lennie: Worst Rangers team I have ever seen in my 70 years of supporting this great club. Not one of them who played tonight [Thursday] deserve to wear the jersey of our great club.

Jim: Five years ago Rangers were in a European final, now we can't even qualify for the third tier European competition. Not only Rangers but Scottish football in general have to address the issues on why we are in freefall.

Brian: An absolute disgrace. The eye-watering amount of money wasted on sixth-rate players is incredible. In my opinion McInnes must win at all costs on Sunday or I personally think he's a goner.
